---
name: accounting
description: "The dashboard, its cells, the runs' records and transcripts, and how cost and time are derived. Read before filling dashboard cells or collecting a run's records."
---

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.
---
name: versioning
description: "Repositories, branches, worktrees, landing under the landing lock, promotion, integration, their lifecycle, and the identity every commit takes. Read before the first commit, and before creating, landing on, promoting or purging any branch or worktree."
---

# Versioning

How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |

The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.

A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
another, so no two module branches collide.

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
way.

## 3. Worktrees

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.

## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and

its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

# Versioning

How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |

The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.

A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
another, so no two module branches collide.

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
way.

## 3. Worktrees

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.

## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.

The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to

[Progress](#44-progress) describes.

### 5.2 Planner runs

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.

recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,

1	//! `deps/llhttp/api.c`: llhttp's public API over its generated parser, ported to Rust.
2	//!
3	//! # The settings
4	//!
5	//! A [`Settings`] is llhttp's table of callbacks, `struct llhttp_settings_s`, which
6	//! `llhttp.h` also names `llhttp_settings_t` and libgit2's `transports/httpparser.h`
7	//! `git_http_parser_settings` ([`SettingsT`], [`HttpParserSettings`]). It has a slot per event
8	//! of a message, each NULL or a callback: a [`Callback`] for an event, such as the start of a
9	//! message or the end of its headers, and a [`DataCallback`] for a run of the input that makes
10	//! up a part of it, such as a header's name or the body. A parser keeps the address of the table
11	//! it is given (`llhttp_init`, [`ParserMut::set_settings`]), and api.c's dispatchers read the
12	//! table on every event of a parse, calling the slot's callback with the parser, or nothing when
13	//! the slot is NULL.
14	//!
15	//! The table owns nothing and holds no context: llhttp's callbacks are handed the parser, whose
16	//! `data` is their context. It keeps its C layout until its `port/layout` stage, since libgit2's
17	//! HTTP client builds one in C, a `static` filled on first use, and hands it to `llhttp_init`.
18	//! A table Rust holds is a plain value, built empty by [`Settings::new`] (`llhttp_settings_init`)
19	//! and filled through [`SettingsMut`]'s setters, one per slot; [`SettingsRef`]'s getters read
20	//! the slots back as the callable types.
21	//!
22	//! # What a table may hold
23	//!
24	//! Each slot is set only from a [`Callback`] or a [`DataCallback`]: a Rust handler behind its
25	//! trampoline, or, inside the crate, a C function that is sound to call with any parser, whatever
26	//! its `data` holds. So every callback of a table Rust builds is sound with every parser, and a
27	//! table installed with [`ParserMut::set_settings`] needs no promise about the parser's `data`:
28	//! that setter is safe, taking a `SettingsRef<'static>`, whose table lives and stays unchanged for
29	//! as long as any parser can keep its address.
30	//!
31	//! A C callback that reads its context through the parser's `data`, as each of libgit2's HTTP
32	//! client's does with its `http_parser_context`, is sound only with the parsers whose `data` it
33	//! expects, so it is no `Callback`, and a table of them is no `Settings` Rust can build. Such a
34	//! table is installed by C, or through the `unsafe` [`ParserMut::set_settings_ptr`], whose caller
35	//! vouches for the parser's `data`, and its callbacks are reached only through the parser that
36	//! holds it, by api.c's dispatchers. That is why the parser's `settings` is read back as the
37	//! address it holds ([`ParserRef::settings_ptr`]), not as a [`SettingsRef`], whose getters
38	//! hand out callbacks callable with any parser.
39	//!
40	//!
41	//! # The parser's API
42	//!
43	//! api.c's functions over a parser are methods of its handles, [`ParserRef`] and
44	//! [`ParserMut`]. Most of them read or write one field, and are that field's accessor in
45	//! `llhttp.rs`, which stands in for both: `llhttp_get_type`, `llhttp_get_method` and
46	//! `llhttp_get_errno` are [`ParserRef::parser_type`], [`ParserRef::method`] and
47	//! [`ParserRef::error`], read as llhttp's enums; `llhttp_get_http_major`,
48	//! `llhttp_get_http_minor`, `llhttp_get_status_code` and `llhttp_get_upgrade` are
49	//! [`ParserRef::http_major`], [`ParserRef::http_minor`], [`ParserRef::status_code`] and
50	//! [`ParserRef::upgrade`]; `llhttp_get_error_reason` and `llhttp_set_error_reason` are
51	//! [`ParserRef::reason`] and [`ParserMut::set_reason`]; and `llhttp_get_error_pos`, whose
52	//! pointer into a past input Rust never follows, is [`ParserRef::error_offset`], which
53	//! locates it in the input it is given. The X-macro generators api.c's name functions
54	//! expand, `HTTP_ERRNO_GEN`, `HTTP_METHOD_GEN` and `HTTP_STATUS_GEN`, turn a map's entry into
55	//! the text its `case` returns, which is [`Errno::constant_name`], [`Method::map_string`]
56	//! and [`Status::map_string`].
57	//!
58	//! What has logic of its own is here: [`ParserMut::execute`] (`llhttp_execute`), the
59	//! pause and its two resumptions ([`ParserMut::pause`], [`ParserMut::resume`],
60	//! [`ParserMut::resume_after_upgrade`]), which move the parser between its running and
61	//! paused states only from the state each expects, the ten lenient setters, each of which
62	//! sets or clears one bit of the lenient flags, and [`ParserRef::debug_trace`]
63	//! (`llhttp__debug`), the trace llhttp's generated parser writes to C's `stderr` when it is
64	//! generated in debug mode, which this build's is not.

68	//! `llhttp_get_error_pos`, `llhttp_get_error_reason`, `llhttp_pause`, `llhttp_resume` and
69	//! `llhttp_resume_after_upgrade`. They are exported, under the module's export feature,
70	//! `ffi-export-deps-llhttp-api-c`, which stays off until api.c switches from C.

121	impl ParserMut<'_> {
122	    /// Parses `data`, the next run of the input, calling the callbacks of the parser's
123	    /// settings as it reads each part of a message: llhttp's entry point, which runs its
124	    /// generated parser, [`parse`](Self::parse), over the run.
125	    ///
126	    /// The parser picks up where the previous run stopped. A pause, by a callback or by
127	    /// [`pause`](Self::pause), or an upgrade stops the run early, at the parser's error
128	    /// position ([`ParserRef::error_offset`]), and each later run returns the same outcome
129	    /// without reading until the parser is resumed.
130	    ///
131	    /// ```
132	    /// use libgit2_crustify::libgit2::deps::llhttp::llhttp::{Parsed, Parser};
133	    ///
134	    /// let mut parser = Parser::new();
135	    /// let response = b"HTTP/1.1 204 No Content\r\n\r\n";
136	    /// assert_eq!(parser.as_mut().execute(response), Ok(Parsed::All));
137	    /// assert_eq!(parser.as_ref().status_code(), 204);
138	    /// ```
139	    ///
140	    /// # Errors
141	    ///
142	    /// The [`ParseError`] the parser stopped at, which it keeps until it is initialised
143	    /// again, as [`parse`](Self::parse) returns it.
144	    ///
145	    /// # Panics
146	    ///
147	    /// As [`parse`](Self::parse): when the parser has no state to run from, where C would
148	    /// abort, and when a callback of the parser's own parse executes it again.
149	    ///
150	    /// Replaces `fn::llhttp_execute`
151	    #[doc(alias = "llhttp_execute")]
152	    pub fn execute(&mut self, data: &[u8]) -> Result<Parsed, ParseError> {
153	        self.parse(data)
154	    }
155	
156	    /// Pauses the parser: a parser with no error takes [`Errno::Paused`], with the reason
157	    /// `"Paused"`, so that its next run returns [`Parsed::Paused`] without reading. A parser
158	    /// that already has an error, a pause among them, keeps it, and its reason.
159	    ///
160	    /// llhttp asks a callback that pauses its parse to return `HPE_PAUSED` rather than call
161	    /// this; libgit2's HTTP client does both at the end of a response's headers. Called from
162	    /// a callback that returns `0`, it leaves the run reading on, and the next run paused.
163	    ///
164	    /// ```
165	    /// use libgit2_crustify::libgit2::deps::llhttp::llhttp::{Errno, Parsed, Parser};
166	    ///
167	    /// let mut parser = Parser::new();
168	    /// parser.as_mut().pause();
169	    /// assert_eq!(parser.as_ref().error(), Ok(Errno::Paused));
170	    /// assert_eq!(parser.as_ref().reason(), Some(c"Paused"));
171	    /// assert_eq!(
172	    ///     parser.as_mut().execute(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"),
173	    ///     Ok(Parsed::Paused)
174	    /// );
175	    /// parser.as_mut().resume();
176	    /// assert_eq!(
177	    ///     parser.as_mut().execute(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"),
178	    ///     Ok(Parsed::All)
179	    /// );
180	    /// ```
181	    ///
182	    /// Replaces `fn::llhttp_pause`
183	    #[doc(alias = "llhttp_pause")]
184	    pub fn pause(&mut self) {
185	        if self.as_ref().error_raw() != 0 {
186	            return;
187	        }
188	        self.set_error(Errno::Paused);
189	        self.set_reason(Some(c"Paused"));
190	    }
191	
192	    /// Resumes a paused parser: one whose error is [`Errno::Paused`] has it cleared, so that
193	    /// its next run reads on from where it stopped. Any other error, an upgrade's pause
194	    /// among them, stays; the reason stays too.
195	    ///
196	    /// Replaces `fn::llhttp_resume`
197	    #[doc(alias = "llhttp_resume")]
198	    pub fn resume(&mut self) {
199	        self.resume_from(Errno::Paused);
200	    }
201	
202	    /// Resumes a parser paused at an upgrade: one whose error is [`Errno::PausedUpgrade`]
203	    /// has it cleared, so that its next run reads what follows as HTTP again. Any other
204	    /// error stays, and the reason too.
205	    ///
206	    /// ```
207	    /// use libgit2_crustify::libgit2::deps::llhttp::llhttp::{Errno, Parsed, Parser};
208	    ///
209	    /// let mut parser = Parser::new();
210	    /// let upgrade = b"HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\nConnection: upgrade\r\n\
211	    ///                 Upgrade: websocket\r\n\r\n";
212	    /// assert_eq!(parser.as_mut().execute(upgrade), Ok(Parsed::PausedUpgrade));
213	    /// parser.as_mut().resume();
214	    /// assert_eq!(parser.as_ref().error(), Ok(Errno::PausedUpgrade));
215	    /// parser.as_mut().resume_after_upgrade();
216	    /// assert_eq!(parser.as_ref().error(), Ok(Errno::Ok));
217	    /// ```
218	    ///
219	    /// Replaces `fn::llhttp_resume_after_upgrade`
220	    #[doc(alias = "llhttp_resume_after_upgrade")]
221	    pub fn resume_after_upgrade(&mut self) {
222	        self.resume_from(Errno::PausedUpgrade);
223	    }
224	
225	    /// Clears the parser's error when it is `pause`, and leaves it otherwise.
226	    fn resume_from(&mut self, pause: Errno) {
227	        if self.as_ref().error_raw() == pause.raw().cast_signed() {
228	            self.set_error(Errno::Ok);
229	        }
230	    }

232	    /// Sets the lenient flag `flag` when `enabled`, and clears it otherwise, leaving the
233	    /// others as they are.
234	    fn set_lenient(&mut self, flag: u16, enabled: bool) {
235	        let flags = self.as_ref().lenient_flags_raw();
236	        self.set_lenient_flags_raw(if enabled { flags | flag } else { flags & !flag });
237	    }
238	}

241	const fn lenient(flag: sys::llhttp_lenient_flags) -> u16 {
242	    let [low, high, 0, 0] = flag.to_le_bytes() else {
243	        panic!("a lenient flag is wider than `lenient_flags`")
244	    };

323	impl ParserRef<'_> {
324	    /// Writes a trace of the parser to C's standard error stream, `stderr`, as llhttp's
325	    /// generated parser does at each step when it is generated in debug mode: the parser's
326	    /// address, its type and flags, the next byte of `rest`, the input still to read (`null`
327	    /// when it is empty), and `msg`, one line in one write:
328	    ///
329	    /// ```text
330	    /// p=0x7ffc3a1c2e40 type=1 flags=00 next=48   debug=on_message_begin
331	    /// ```
332	    ///
333	    /// The line goes through C's stream, in order with what the remaining C writes there.
334	    /// `type` is printed in decimal and the flags and the byte in hexadecimal, two digits at
335	    /// least. A byte of 0x80 or more is printed as two digits, where C, which prints a
336	    /// signed `char` through `%02x`, prints it sign-extended to an `unsigned int`
337	    /// (`ffffff80`), a value `%x` is not defined for.
338	    ///
339	    /// # Errors
340	    ///
341	    /// When `msg` holds a NUL byte, which C's stream cannot carry, or the write fails, as
342	    /// [`FileRef::print`](glibc_bindings::libc::libio::genops::FileRef::print) reports it.
343	    ///
344	    /// Replaces `fn::llhttp__debug`
345	    #[doc(alias = "llhttp__debug")]
346	    pub fn debug_trace(&self, rest: &[u8], msg: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
347	        ffi_import::print_to_stderr(&self.debug_line(rest, msg))
348	    }
349	
350	    /// The line [`debug_trace`](Self::debug_trace) writes, its newline included.
351	    ///
352	    /// It is built from its parts, without `format_args!`, whose expansion holds an
353	    /// `unsafe` block outside the module's regions.
354	    fn debug_line(&self, rest: &[u8], msg: &str) -> String {
355	        let mut line = String::from("p=0x");
356	        push_hex(&mut line, self.as_ptr().addr(), 1);
357	        line.push_str(" type=");
358	        line.push_str(&self.parser_type_raw().to_string());
359	        line.push_str(" flags=");
360	        push_hex(&mut line, usize::from(self.flags_raw()), 2);
361	        match rest.first() {
362	            None => line.push_str(" next=null"),
363	            Some(&next) => {
364	                line.push_str(" next=");
365	                push_hex(&mut line, usize::from(next), 2);
366	                line.push_str("  ");
367	            }
368	        }
369	        line.push_str(" debug=");
370	        line.push_str(msg);
371	        line.push('\n');
372	        line
373	    }
374	}

376	/// Appends `value` in lowercase hexadecimal, at least `digits` digits, zero-padded, as
377	/// printf's `%0<digits>x` and `%p`'s digits print it.
378	fn push_hex(line: &mut String, value: usize, digits: usize) {
379	    let width = usize::try_from(value.bit_width().div_ceil(4)).unwrap_or(digits);
380	    for i in (0..width.max(digits)).rev() {
381	        let nibble = (value >> (i * 4)) & 0xF;
382	        line.push(char::from(b"0123456789abcdef"[nibble]));
383	    }
384	}

458	    /// Writes `text` to C's standard error stream, `stderr`, in one `fprintf` under the
459	    /// stream's lock, as `llhttp__debug`'s `fprintf(stderr, …)` does.
460	    ///
461	    /// # Errors
462	    ///
463	    /// Those of `FileRef::print`: a NUL byte in `text`, or the write's failure.
464	    pub(super) fn print_to_stderr(text: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
465	        // SAFETY: the stream is borrowed for this call alone, as C's `fprintf(stderr, …)`
466	        // borrows it, and asks of the program what that expression asks. No C of libgit2, of
467	        // its bundled dependencies or of its tests assigns `stderr`, closes it, reopens it, or
468	        // writes it but through stdio's locking routines (`fprintf`, `fputs`, `vfprintf`): none
469	        // calls `fclose`, `freopen` or `__fsetlocking` on it, nor an `_unlocked` routine, so
470	        // that no write of `stderr` races with the read, the stream stays open for the call,
471	        // and every other access to it holds its lock. Rust's `std::io::stderr` writes the
472	        // descriptor, not the stream.
473	        let stream = unsafe { stderr() };
474	        stream.print(text).map(drop)

2392	            // is C's own, from `llhttp__internal_init` or an earlier run: no accessor writes
2393	            // `_current`, `_index` or the span fields. It is either in error, which the call
2394	            // returns without running, or has a state to run from (checked above), so C's
2395	            // `abort` on `s_error` is not reached. `range` bounds `data`, which is live and
2396	            // unchanged for the call; C reads only within it, keeps `_span_pos0` and
2397	            // `error_pos` pointing into it, and never follows either after the call: the
2398	            // next run restarts an open span at its own input, and `error_pos` is never
2399	            // followed by Rust. The settings' callbacks are NULL, or sound to call with this
2400	            // parser and its `data` (`set_settings_ptr`'s and `set_data`'s contracts), and
2401	            // none of them parses or initialises the parser again from Rust (`Executing`).
2402	            let code = unsafe {
2403	                sys::llhttp__internal_execute(parser, range.start.cast(), range.end.cast())
2404	            };
2405	            ParseError::outcome(code)
2406	        }
2407	    }
2408	
2409	    /// `llhttp_cb`'s function type: what a [`Callback`] holds and `llhttp.h`'s settings
2410	    /// slots point to.
2411	    type CallbackFn = unsafe extern "C" fn(*mut sys::llhttp_t) -> c_int;
2412	
2413	    /// `llhttp_data_cb`'s function type: what a [`DataCallback`] holds and `llhttp.h`'s
2414	    /// settings slots point to.
2415	    type DataCallbackFn = unsafe extern "C" fn(*mut sys::llhttp_t, *const c_char, usize) -> c_int;
2416	
2417	    /// An event callback (`llhttp_cb`): the C function a parser's settings name for an
2418	    /// event of a message, such as its start or the end of its headers, which C calls with
2419	    /// the parser being parsed.
2420	    ///
2421	    /// Built over an [`EventHandler`] with [`new`](Self::new), whose `extern "C"`
2422	    /// trampoline hands the handler the parser's exclusive handle and catches its panics,
2423	    /// or, inside the crate, over a C function, which its `unsafe` constructor vouches is
2424	    /// sound to call with any parser. Either way [`call`](Self::call) is safe. A function
2425	    /// pointer and nothing else: `Copy`, owning nothing, never released, and callable from
2426	    /// any thread.
2427	    ///
2428	    /// ```
2429	    /// use std::ffi::c_int;
2430	    ///
2431	    /// use libgit2_crustify::libgit2::deps::llhttp::llhttp::{
2432	    ///     Callback, EventHandler, Parser, ParserMut,
2433	    /// };
2434	    ///
2435	    /// struct Upgrading;
2436	    ///
2437	    /// impl EventHandler for Upgrading {
2438	    ///     fn on_event(mut parser: ParserMut<'_>) -> c_int {
2439	    ///         parser.set_upgrade(true);
2440	    ///         0
2441	    ///     }
2442	    /// }
2443	    ///
2444	    /// const CALLBACK: Callback = Callback::new::<Upgrading>();
2445	    /// let mut parser = Parser::new();
2446	    /// assert_eq!(CALLBACK.call(parser.as_mut()), 0);
2447	    /// assert!(parser.as_ref().upgrade());
2448	    /// assert!(CALLBACK.raw().is_some());
2449	    /// ```
2450	    ///
2451	    /// Its function is private: only `new` builds one outside the crate.
2452	    ///
2453	    /// ```compile_fail,E0423
2454	    /// use libgit2_crustify::libgit2::deps::llhttp::llhttp::Callback;
2455	    /// use libgit2_crustify::sys::libgit2 as sys;
2456	    ///
2457	    /// unsafe extern "C" fn c_callback(_: *mut sys::llhttp_t) -> std::ffi::c_int {
2458	    ///     0
2459	    /// }
2460	    /// let _ = Callback(c_callback);
2461	    /// ```
2462	    ///
2463	    /// Wraps `fnp::llhttp_cb`
2464	    #[doc(alias = "llhttp_cb")]
2465	    #[derive(Clone, Copy)]
2466	    pub struct Callback(CallbackFn);
2467	
2468	    impl Callback {
2469	        /// The callback that hands C's calls to `H`.
2470	        #[must_use]
2471	        pub const fn new<H: EventHandler>() -> Self {
2472	            Self(event_with::<H>)
2473	        }
2474	
2475	        /// The callback over a C function.
2476	        ///
2477	        /// # Safety
2478	        ///
2479	        /// For as long as this value or a copy of it lives, `f` must be sound to call with
2480	        /// every live, exclusively held parser, in any state and whatever its `data` and
2481	        /// `settings` hold, on the thread that holds the parser, and must not unwind: those
2482	        /// are the calls [`call`](Self::call) makes, and those of the parsers a
2483	        /// [`Settings`](crate::libgit2::deps::llhttp::api::Settings) holding it is given. A C
2484	        /// callback that reads the parser's `data` as its own context does not meet this,
2485	        /// and is reached through the settings its parser executes with instead, stored by
2486	        /// [`ParserMut::set_settings_ptr`], whose contract vouches for it.
2487	        pub(crate) const unsafe fn from_fn(f: CallbackFn) -> Self {
2488	            Self(f)
2489	        }
2490	
2491	        /// Calls the callback with `parser`, as llhttp does, and returns what it returns.
2492	        #[must_use = "the callback's return tells the parse how to go on"]
2493	        pub fn call(self, mut parser: ParserMut<'_>) -> c_int {
2494	            // SAFETY: `parser` addresses a live parser this exclusive handle lends for the
2495	            // call: `CallbackFn`'s only argument. `new`'s trampolines need nothing more, and
2496	            // `from_fn`'s caller vouched that the function is sound with any such parser.
2497	            unsafe { (self.0)(parser.as_mut_ptr()) }
2498	        }
2499	
2500	        /// The C value, as a settings slot holds it: never NULL.
2501	        #[must_use]
2502	        pub const fn raw(self) -> sys::llhttp_cb {
2503	            Some(self.0)
2504	        }
2505	    }
2506	
2507	    impl fmt::Debug for Callback {
2508	        fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
2509	            f.debug_tuple("Callback")
2510	                .field(&(self.0 as *const ()))
2511	                .finish()
2512	        }
2513	    }
2514	
2515	    /// `llhttp_cb` over [`EventHandler::on_event`].
2516	    ///
2517	    /// # Safety
2518	    ///
2519	    /// `parser` is NULL or addresses a live parser nothing else accesses for the call but
2520	    /// the handles this call makes: llhttp's call with the parser it is parsing, and
2521	    /// [`Callback::call`]'s.
2522	    unsafe extern "C" fn event_with<H: EventHandler>(parser: *mut sys::llhttp_t) -> c_int {
2523	        // SAFETY: per this function's contract, a non-NULL `parser` is a live parser lent
2524	        // to the call alone; the handle's borrow ends with the call.
2525	        let Some(parser) = (unsafe { ParserMut::from_ptr(parser) }) else {
2526	            return -1;
2527	        };
2528	        callback::barrier(|| H::on_event(parser), || -1)
2529	    }
2530	
2531	    /// A data callback (`llhttp_data_cb`): the C function a parser's settings name for a
2532	    /// run of the input that makes up a part of a message, such as its URL, a header's
2533	    /// name or value, or its body, which C calls with the parser and the run.
2534	    ///
2535	    /// Built over a [`DataHandler`] with [`new`](Self::new), whose trampoline hands the
2536	    /// handler the parser's handle and the run as a slice borrowed for the call, or, inside
2537	    /// the crate, over a C function, as [`Callback`] is. A part may come in several runs,
2538	    /// one per call, when it spans several parses. A function pointer and nothing else.
2539	    ///
2540	    /// ```
2541	    /// use std::cell::RefCell;
2542	    /// use std::ffi::c_int;
2543	    ///
2544	    /// use libgit2_crustify::libgit2::deps::llhttp::llhttp::{DataCallback, DataHandler, Parser, ParserMut};
2545	    ///
2546	    /// thread_local!(static SEEN: RefCell<Vec<u8>> = const { RefCell::new(Vec::new()) });
2547	    ///
2548	    /// struct Collect;
2549	    ///
2550	    /// impl DataHandler for Collect {
2551	    ///     fn on_data(_: ParserMut<'_>, data: &[u8]) -> c_int {
2552	    ///         SEEN.with_borrow_mut(|seen| seen.extend_from_slice(data));
2553	    ///         0
2554	    ///     }
2555	    /// }
2556	    ///
2557	    /// const CALLBACK: DataCallback = DataCallback::new::<Collect>();
2558	    /// let mut parser = Parser::new();
2559	    /// assert_eq!(CALLBACK.call(parser.as_mut(), b"Host"), 0);
2560	    /// assert_eq!(SEEN.with_borrow(Vec::clone), b"Host");
2561	    /// ```
2562	    ///
2563	    /// Wraps `fnp::llhttp_data_cb`
2564	    #[doc(alias = "llhttp_data_cb")]
2565	    #[derive(Clone, Copy)]
2566	    pub struct DataCallback(DataCallbackFn);
2567	
2568	    impl DataCallback {
2569	        /// The callback that hands C's calls to `H`.
2570	        #[must_use]
2571	        pub const fn new<H: DataHandler>() -> Self {
2572	            Self(data_with::<H>)
2573	        }
2574	
2575	        /// The callback over a C function.
2576	        ///
2577	        /// # Safety
2578	        ///
2579	        /// As [`Callback::from_fn`]'s, the calls being [`call`](Self::call)'s: with every
2580	        /// live, exclusively held parser, and a run of bytes live and unchanged for the
2581	        /// call, its start and its length.
2582	        pub(crate) const unsafe fn from_fn(f: DataCallbackFn) -> Self {
2583	            Self(f)
2584	        }
2585	
2586	        /// Calls the callback with `parser` and `data`, as llhttp does, and returns what it
2587	        /// returns.
2588	        #[must_use = "the callback's return tells the parse how to go on"]
2589	        pub fn call(self, mut parser: ParserMut<'_>, data: &[u8]) -> c_int {
2590	            // SAFETY: `parser` addresses a live parser this exclusive handle lends for the
2591	            // call, and `data` a run of `data.len()` bytes live and unchanged for it:
2592	            // `DataCallbackFn`'s arguments. `new`'s trampolines need nothing more, and
2593	            // `from_fn`'s caller vouched for the function with any such arguments.
2594	            unsafe { (self.0)(parser.as_mut_ptr(), data.as_ptr().cast(), data.len()) }
2595	        }
2596	
2597	        /// The C value, as a settings slot holds it: never NULL.
2598	        #[must_use]
2599	        pub const fn raw(self) -> sys::llhttp_data_cb {
2600	            Some(self.0)
2601	        }
2602	    }
2603	
2604	    impl fmt::Debug for DataCallback {
2605	        fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
2606	            f.debug_tuple("DataCallback")
2607	                .field(&(self.0 as *const ()))
2608	                .finish()
2609	        }
2610	    }
2611	
2612	    /// `llhttp_data_cb` over [`DataHandler::on_data`].
2613	    ///
2614	    /// # Safety
2615	    ///
2616	    /// As [`event_with`]'s for `parser`; and `at` is NULL or addresses `length` bytes live
2617	    /// and unchanged for the call: llhttp's span, from its start to where it read, within
2618	    /// the input of the parse, or [`DataCallback::call`]'s slice.
2619	    unsafe extern "C" fn data_with<H: DataHandler>(
2620	        parser: *mut sys::llhttp_t,
2621	        at: *const c_char,
2622	        length: usize,
2623	    ) -> c_int {
2624	        // SAFETY: per this function's contract, a non-NULL `parser` is a live parser lent
2625	        // to the call alone; the handle's borrow ends with the call.
2626	        let Some(parser) = (unsafe { ParserMut::from_ptr(parser) }) else {
2627	            return -1;
2628	        };
2629	        let data: &[u8] = if length == 0 {
2630	            &[]
2631	        } else if at.is_null() {
2632	            return -1;
2633	        } else {
2634	            // SAFETY: per this function's contract, a non-NULL `at` addresses `length`
2635	            // initialised bytes, which nothing writes or frees for the call, the slice's
2636	            // borrow; `u8` is aligned to 1.
2637	            unsafe { core::slice::from_raw_parts(at.cast::<u8>(), length) }
2638	        };
2639	        callback::barrier(|| H::on_data(parser, data), || -1)
2640	    }
2641	}

### `libgit2/src/util/utf8.c` integration: the switch from C

The campaign's first switch, run by `modules/libgit2/src/util/utf8.c/integration/run-1` on the
module's branch after the merge of the working branch (`43605086f`): `012d1d34c`, and the
fork's `1b37e3d08`. The export feature `ffi-export-src-util-utf8-c` is deleted, the crate's
only one, so `utf8.rs`'s gateway compiles from now on, and its four `unit_priv` tests run in
`lib`. The module's six `equiv` tests are retired with the C they compared
(`tests/equiv/src/util/utf8.rs`); their cases stay in its unit tests and doctests. The raw
bindings of `git_utf8_iterate`, `git_utf8_char_length` and `git_utf8_valid_buf_length` stay,
and now reach the exports. `src/util/utf8.c` leaves `c/`: the change is the commit
`integrate src/util/utf8.c` on a local `fork/main`, which stands for
`crustify-rs/libgit2-fork`'s `main` and is not pushed, and `.gitmodules` names the fork.
`utf8.h` stays for `path.c`, `diff_xdiff.c` and `fs_path.c`. The module's tied C test,
`tests/util/utf8.c`, calls `git_utf8_char_length` alone, so it stays and checks the export.
No C test leaves, so no case needs listing. The exports are a private module's, so the
crate's API does not change.

The switch also made the one-time change of the C build. The fork's
`cmake/SelectRust.cmake` links the static library that `LIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY` names wherever
the remaining C is linked: `libgit2.so`, the CLI, `libgit2_tests` and `util_tests`. It is an
imported target among `LIBGIT2_SYSTEM_LIBS`. `libgit2.so` keeps the Rust's symbols local
(`--exclude-libs`). Its dynamic symbols are the previous generation's on every variant,
`asan-ubsan`'s two linker-made `__start_`/`__stop_asan_globals` aside. Those come from LLVM
23's instrumentation of the Rust and are protected. Without the variable, the library leaves
the three exports undefined, as the crate's bundled and shared builds of `c/` need. Each
variant's `build` command first makes the library (`crustify/scripts/rust-staticlib.sh`),
between `configure` and the C's link. It builds the crate of the checkout that runs it as a
`staticlib` on the dev profile, the profile the Rust tests run on, so that the C tests check
the same build with debug assertions and overflow checks on. It builds in campaign mode
against the configured variant, with `--features bindgen`, so that the committed bindings
are checked, and with `CRUSTIFY_STATICLIB`, under which `build.rs` reads the build's
configuration and links none of its C. It instruments the Rust as `cargo-variant.sh` does.
`nm` shows that the library defines only the Rust, the three exports and the crate's
`__extern` wrappers, and no libgit2 C. Every other campaign build leaves the library out of
its link, matched by canonical path, so that no binary holds the Rust twice. BSan has no
`cargo bsan rustc`, so a stand-in for the cargo it runs turns its `build` into `rustc
--crate-type staticlib`. The BSan runtime its driver bundles is removed from the copy, since
the variant's C link links it.

The variants were rebuilt as a new generation, `crustify/builds.gen1`, with
`crustify/scripts/build-variants.sh`, and this worktree's `crustify/builds` links to it.
`crustify/builds` itself, which three batches were using, was left untouched. Each variant is
configured from the generation's own `c`, a detached worktree of the fork at `1b37e3d08`, so

### `libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c` wave 194 batch 0: `llhttp.c`'s types ahead of api.c

A wrap batch ahead of its consumer: `deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s five types, which api.c's
`port` waves use, bound in llhttp.c's own file, `src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs`, which
its wave 238 ports. `st::llhttp__internal_s` is `Parser`, a `define_ctype!` layout with
`ParserRef` and `ParserMut`, and its typedefs `llhttp__internal_t`, `llhttp_t` and
`git_http_parser` are the aliases `InternalT`, `LlhttpT` and `HttpParser`. A parser owns
nothing and C keeps no pointer to one, so it is a plain value: `CZeroable`, with no owner or
policy; its constructor, `llhttp__internal_init` through `llhttp_init`, is the next batch's.
The closed enums `llhttp_errno`, `llhttp_method`, `llhttp_status` and `llhttp_type` are
`Errno`, `Method`, `Status` and `ParserType`, 185 variants over bindgen's constants with
fallible conversions and an `Unnamed*` error each, their typedefs aliases (`ErrnoT`, …).

The `fields` cell counts the 21 assigned. 15 have accessors: the fields api.c, http.c,
`transports/httpclient.c` and `transports/httpparser.c` touch. The other six, `_index`,
`_span_pos0`, `_span_cb0`, `_current`, `header_state` and `initial_message_completed`, only
llhttp.c's generated code reads or writes (`query structs --field-touchers`), and three of
them would send it through a wild pointer or out of a table if written from outside, so they
have none (`crustify/evolution/wrap-ahead-field-users`). The fields holding an enum's value
are read typed and fallibly, and raw (`*_raw`) as api.c's getters return them; the flag words
and `finish` raw, until `llhttp_flags`, `llhttp_lenient_flags` and `llhttp_finish` are bound.
`reason` is lent as a `&CStr` for the handle's borrow and set only from a `&'static CStr`;
`error_pos` is never followed, only compared with a caller's slice (`error_offset`); `data`
and `settings` are read as addresses and set through the batch's two `unsafe fn`s, whose
contracts carry what the callbacks read through them. Those four are the boundary scan's
sites in the changeset: no safe form replaces a user's untyped context, and `settings`'
typed getter waits for `llhttp_settings_s`, api.c's item, which the cycle through
`llhttp_cb` puts after this batch (T3 drops the cast edge). The pointer findings of the
struct's eight pointer fields, and `llhttp__internal_init`'s and `llhttp_init`'s `init`
roles, are in the ownership store.

The raw bindings gain `llhttp.h` in `wrapper.h`, the five types with their typedefs, and
api.c's `llhttp_init`, `llhttp_settings_init`, `llhttp_execute` and nine getters, which the
equivalence tests compare with; `llhttp_settings_s` and the callback typedefs come in with
them. Tests: 12 `unit_pub` (the enums' values and errors, every setter against its getter),
4 `ub_safe` (reborrows, a lent reason, parsers moved in a `Vec`), 6 `ub_unsafe` (one suite
per `unsafe` setter: callbacks reading the stored context through C, a context replaced
between calls, NULL settings, a table that ignores `data`), 8 `equiv` (two parsers fed the
same input by `llhttp_execute`, one read through api.c's getters and one through the
handles, compared after every step: a response in pieces, an unnamed status, requests with
their method and upgrade, an invalid message, a callback's own error, a pause and resume, the
lenient flags, the setters' effect on the C) and 5 compile-fail doctests. llhttp has no C
tests of its own in the tree.

Coverage was measured with `crustify/scripts/coverage/run.sh` on a `git archive` of the wave
tip `2216b0cd0` and on this tree, each suite alone, and read with `report.py` from the
scratch tree's `src/libgit2`, the unit column merging `lib` and `unit_pub`. The tip's Rust
figures are the recorded ones; its C figures read `27.92`% (`ub_safe`), `19.08`%
(`ub_unsafe`), `42.51`% (`equiv`), `31.37`% (unit) and `44.98`% (total), against which the pp
cells are taken. The C total moves
by `+1.12` pp: the equivalence and unsafe-setter tests run llhttp's parser, which nothing
reached before (`llhttp.c` 18.64% of lines, `http.c` 78.35%, `api.c` 11.99%). Worklist:
`llhttp.rs` 110 of 110 lines, 33 of 33 functions, 147 of 148 regions; the region missed,
`error_offset`'s return for a position before the slice, has an assertion added after the
measurement. Of the parser's states the tests reach the initialised, parsing, paused,
upgrade-paused and failed ones, and the transitions between them that the setters and
`llhttp_execute` make. The Overview's Rust LoC moves by ffimap's `code.loc.total` (`+919`)
and `code.tests.loc.total` (`+683`); `wrapped types` counts the five against the recorded
`258`.

The safety audit scans (ffimap `9aa2ef1`, `--ffibox`, `--sys-crates pcre2_sys`, the 13 seams,
`--regions ffi_import,ffi_export`): `pub raw ptr`, `pub void ptr` and `pub unsafe fn` are the
two getters and two setters above, `raw→std` the reason's `CStr::from_ptr`, `C by value`
three mentions of `llhttp__internal_s` by value in the layout and its handles' seams, and the
raw derefs and unsafe blocks the accessors' one-operation projections and reads. The four
`unsafe` blocks the first scan found outside the regions were the `Unnamed*` errors' `write!`
(std's `format_args!`, which ffimap counts); their `Display` writes its parts instead, as
`basics.rs`'s `UnnamedHashId` does. `ffimap api` against the tip: the five items are `new`, as
are all 212 anchor keys of the file (the 185 constants, 15 fields and 7 typedefs with them),
and every unattributed module is `kept` but the raw `sys::libgit2`, `extended`.

Gates, on the base `2216b0cd0`, the wave branch's tip when the batch landed: the workspace is
formatted, and `clippy --all-targets` passes with warnings denied on `plain`. The whole
workspace passes on `plain` (`lib` 840 and 1 ignored, `ub_safe` 766, `ub_unsafe` 126,
`equiv` 536, `unit_pub` 79, `hidden_symbols` 1, doctests 72 merged and 383 standalone). The
batch's tests pass under ASan+UBSan, and its `unit_pub` and `ub_safe` tests under Miri; each
`equiv` and `ub_unsafe` test was run alone there and stops at `llhttp_init` or
